intro: Writer's block when stuck on a first draft usually comes from fatigue, low motivation, or fear of a bad sentence, not from a lack of ideas. A good first step is to restart at your last sentence, set a small session target, and accept a rough page for now. Below you will find what the stall costs, why it happens, fixes that cost nothing, and where Lazur helps on a Mac.
tldr: Writer's block on a first draft is widely reported, but no source I opened gives a reliable rate for all writers.
A 2022 study of 146 writers found physiological, motivational, cognitive, and behavioral causes.
Free fixes include restarting mid-sentence, switching projects, writing badly on purpose, and setting a session target.
Scrivener 3.5.2 on Mac has separate project and session targets, which is the most direct built-in tracking I found.
Lazur can dictate rough text at your cursor and answer questions about your screen. It does not write the draft for you.

blocks.text: Writer's block on a first draft has a recognizable pattern. You open the file, read the last paragraph, and then nothing comes. Or words come, and you delete them before the sentence ends. The draft stays the same length for days, and the blank space at the end starts to feel like a judgment. That stall is what this page covers.
What writer's block costs you on a first draft

Be honest about the cost before you pick a fix. The numbers below are thin, so read them with care. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median annual wage of $76,910 for writers and authors in May 2025. That is about $36.98 per hour. The figure excludes self-employed workers, and many writers work for themselves. The same source projects 0% change in employment from 2025 to 2035.

Book income is a different measure. The Authors Guild's 2023 Author Income Survey covers 2022. It reports a median of $10,000 from books for full-time authors. Including other author-related income, the median rises to $20,000. The survey drew 5,699 published authors, but the page reports no response rate. That makes it a self-selected sample, so treat it as a rough picture, not a census.

blocks.title: The gap in the data
blocks.text: No source I opened measured writer's block directly. None counts the hours lost, the grades affected, or the deadlines missed. Use pay figures as background, not as proof of what one stall costs you.
Why writer's block happens on a first draft

The most useful study of working writers I found is Ahmed and Güss (2022). The authors ran an online mixed-method survey of 146 writers, including professional and semiprofessional writers. Those writers described four kinds of cause: physiological, motivational, cognitive, and behavioral. Physiological and motivational causes were the most common. The page does not give per-cause percentages, so do not quote one.

Those four categories help you match a cause to a fix. A tired body needs rest, not a new outline. A dull draft needs a reason to return, not a pep talk. A planning habit needs a rule, such as no structure changes until the scene is written. Trying every fix at once wastes the session. Pick the cause that fits your last stall.

A common mistake is to treat all stalls as one problem. People add more research when they are tired. Others add more coffee when they are scared of a bad page. Notice what happened in the minute before you stopped. That minute tells you more than a list of causes.
Fixes you can use today without buying anything

None of these fixes needs a new app. Most are habits you can start in the document you already have. The evidence behind each one varies, and the text says so. Start with the fix that matches the cause you noticed, then test it for a few sessions before you judge it.
Restart in the middle of a sentence

Writers in the Ahmed and Güss study described taking a break as a solution. A break works better when you prepare for it. Before you stop, leave the cursor in the middle of a sentence or on a line you know how to finish. When you return, finish that line. Skip rereading the whole chapter. Restarting at a known point beats starting over.
Work on a second project for a while

Working on a different project was another solution writers described. Keep a side file for scene notes, a short essay, or research you enjoy. Give it a set block of time, then return to the stuck draft. The side file lets you leave the draft without abandoning it. The evidence here is self-report only, so judge it by your own sessions.
Write badly on purpose

Forcing yourself to keep writing was also reported as a solution. Make a rule for one session: weak sentences count. Put gaps in brackets, such as [check the year] or [the sister's name]. Brackets let you move on without solving every problem now. Freewriting is a close cousin, where you type without stopping or editing. I found no controlled evidence that freewriting fixes writer's block, so treat it as an experiment, not a cure.
Talk the idea through with someone

Discussing ideas with others also appeared on the list of solutions. A friend, a writing partner, or a short call can make the plot real. Keep the talk short. You want a listener, not a rewrite. A 2021 study tested a 15-day writing group program with graduate psychology students writing theses. Thesis procrastination scores fell from a pretest mean of 72.30 to 62.00. That study had no control group, so it shows a hopeful sign, not proof.
Plan the trigger, not the feeling

An if-then plan names when you will start and what you will do. For example: if it is after lunch, then I write one paragraph before I open email. A 2006 meta-analysis by Gollwitzer and Sheeran found that implementation intentions had a medium-to-large positive effect on goal attainment. The analysis covered 94 independent tests. It addressed goals in general, not writing. Publication bias may inflate the estimate, so the plan is a cheap test, not a guarantee.
Set a session target in Scrivener

Open Project > Show Project Targets. You can set a project target and a session target separately. The toolbar then shows progress lines above and below Quick Search. Literature & Latte describes this in its guide. The latest Mac release I could confirm is Scrivener 3.5.2, dated 18 December 2025. Check the Literature & Latte pricing page before you buy, because I did not open a current price.

If you draft in Pages, Word, or Google Docs, you can use the same idea without Scrivener. Write down one session goal before you open the file. Check the word count in your app when you finish. Keep the goal small enough that you can finish it on a bad day. A goal you meet teaches you more than a big goal you abandon.
A worked example of a stalled first draft

This example is made up, but the pattern is common. A writer has a mystery novel draft that stopped at the midpoint. Every new scene felt wrong. The writer then tried to outline the rest before writing it. The outline became a second stall, with more notes and no new pages.

The fix came in a few moves, in this order. First, the writer stopped editing the earlier chapters, which had become a safe place to hide. Second, the writer set a session target for the day, and a project target for the book. Third, the writer wrote the stuck scene as a bracketed summary, then moved to the next scene. Within a week, the midpoint had a rough version. It was not good. It was finished, and that made the next scene easier to start.
Mistakes that keep the block going

items: Rereading the whole draft before you write anything new.
Editing the first chapter over and over because it feels safe.
Setting a target for the whole book, not for one session.
Waiting for the right mood before you open the file.
Leaving the draft for weeks, then trying to restart at the top.
Reorganizing folders or outlines when the real problem is one scene.

blocks.text: Each of these feels productive while you do it. That is why they keep the block going. If you catch yourself doing one, close the earlier chapter, go to your last line, and write one sentence. Then stop or continue, your choice.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. A one-week routine for your first draft
Use this week as a test, not a promise. Each day has one job. Stop after the job, even if you want more. Stopping while the next line is clear makes the next session easier to start.
Edge cases to check before you change tools

Sometimes the stall is not writer's block. If you lack a fact for a scene, research it before you write the scene. If you write for a client, a patient, or an employer, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data before you dictate or paste anything into an AI tool. Those rules outrank any tip on this page.

If the stall lasts for weeks, and comes with low mood, poor sleep, or constant exhaustion, talk to a doctor or counselor. A writing fix will not treat a health problem. Physiological causes were among the most common in the Ahmed and Güss study, so check your sleep and health as part of the fix.
Next steps for Mac writers

Start in the app you already use. [Pages for writers on Mac](/for/writers/pages) covers templates, drafts, and voice help. [Word for writers on Mac](/for/writers/word) covers long drafts and dictation. [Google Docs for writers on Mac](/for/writers/google-docs) covers shortcuts and offline editing. If you keep outlines in Notion, [AI assistant for Notion on Mac](/apps/notion) covers voice help for pages.

Pick the fix that matches the cause you noticed. Run it for one session, then check the result in your word count or session target. If it helped, keep it for the next session. If it did not, try the next fix on the list.

faq.question: Is writer's block a real condition?
faq.answer: Writers report it widely, and researchers have studied it in working writers. The sources I opened describe causes and self-reported solutions, not a clinical diagnosis. If the stall comes with low mood or exhaustion, see a doctor.

faq.question: How common is writer's block?
faq.answer: No rigorous rate for all writers appears in the sources I opened. A figure of 94% circulates online, but it comes from a university student survey, not from working writers. Do not quote it as a rate for writers.

faq.question: How much do writers earn?
faq.answer: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median annual wage of $76,910 for writers and authors in May 2025. That figure excludes self-employed workers. The Authors Guild reports a 2022 median book income of $10,000 for full-time authors.

faq.question: Does freewriting fix writer's block?
faq.answer: I found no controlled evidence that it does. Writers describe it as useful, but that is self-report. Try it for one session, then judge the result by how much you wrote.

faq.question: What is an if-then plan?
faq.answer: It names a trigger and an action, such as: if it is after lunch, then I write one paragraph before checking email. A 2006 meta-analysis found this approach helped people reach goals in general. It did not test writing specifically.

faq.question: Can Lazur write my first draft?
faq.answer: No. Lazur dictates, drafts, and types text when you ask, and it answers questions about your screen out loud. You decide what stays. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur with client or patient material?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules on client or patient data first. Lazur sends audio and screenshots to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Check your rules before you dictate or share sensitive text.

faq.question: Does Lazur run on Windows?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.

costs.title: Pay and time at risk
costs.text: The BLS median annual wage for writers and authors was $76,910 in May 2025, but self-employed writers are not in that figure. Time lost to a stalled draft does not appear in any source I opened. Count your own sessions for one week to see what the stall costs you.

costs.title: Book income is often modest
costs.text: The Authors Guild reports a $10,000 median book income for full-time authors in 2022, and $20,000 with other author-related income. That sample was self-selected, and no response rate was reported. A stalled draft delays income, but the sources do not measure by how much.

costs.title: Deadlines and grades
costs.text: No source I opened measured how writer's block affects deadlines, grades, or the quality of finished work. Be wary of any site that gives a precise figure without a link to its method. Your own calendar is a better test than a generic statistic.

costs.title: Energy and confidence
costs.text: Ahmed and Güss describe physiological and motivational causes that can drain energy and confidence. A stall can then make the next session harder. None of the sources I opened measured this cost, so treat it as a pattern to watch, not a proven loss.

causes.title: Physiological: a tired or stressed body
causes.text: Ahmed and Güss (2022) found physiological causes among the most common in their sample of 146 writers. Tiredness, stress, and poor sleep can all make a sentence feel heavier than it is. When your body is flat, a plan that needs focus will fail. Notice the pattern before you blame your skill.

causes.title: Motivational: no reason to keep going
causes.text: The same study found motivational causes among the most common. A draft that feels like a chore gives you no pull to return. A distant goal, such as a finished book, can feel too far away to act on. The next step stays vague, so the next session never starts.

causes.title: Cognitive: planning too early
causes.text: Ahmed and Güss list cognitive causes too. Many writers try to fix structure, names, and facts before the first draft exists. Each change then forces a rewrite of earlier pages. The result is planning that looks like work but produces no new sentences.

causes.title: Behavioral: habits that pull you away
causes.text: Behavioral causes are the habits around the draft. Email, news, and research tabs open before the document does. Each switch costs attention. The blank page then feels bigger when you return to it.

causes.title: Fear of a bad first sentence
causes.text: This one is my reading of the pattern, not a separate finding in the study. You hold each sentence to final-draft standards. The first draft then becomes a test you can fail, so you avoid it. Writing badly on purpose is the direct answer to this cause.

fixes.title: Restart at your last sentence
fixes.text: Writers in the Ahmed and Güss study reported taking a break as a solution. Before you leave, end the session in the middle of a sentence. The next session then starts with a line you already know. Restarting at a known point beats starting over.

fixes.title: Work on a second project for a while
fixes.text: Respondents also described switching to a different project. Keep a side file for essays, scene notes, or research. Spend a set block there, then return to the draft. The evidence for this is self-report only, so test it on your own sessions.

fixes.title: Write badly on purpose
fixes.text: Forcing yourself to keep writing was another reported solution. Allow weak sentences and bracketed gaps such as [check the date]. Freewriting, typing without stopping, is a related method. I found no controlled study showing that it fixes writer's block.

fixes.title: Talk the idea through with someone
fixes.text: Discussing ideas with others appeared on the list of solutions. A partner, friend, or writing group gives you a listener. A 2021 study of a 15-day writing group program showed lower procrastination scores, but it had no control group, so the result is only a hopeful sign.

fixes.title: Make an if-then plan
fixes.text: Name the trigger and the action in advance. A 2006 meta-analysis of 94 tests found implementation intentions had a medium-to-large positive effect on goal attainment. It covered goals in general, not writing. Test the plan for a week and keep it only if it helps.

fixes.title: Set a session target in Scrivener
fixes.text: In Scrivener 3.5.2 for Mac, open Project > Show Project Targets. Set a session target and a project target. Progress lines then appear above and below Quick Search. Scrivener is paid software, so check the Literature & Latte pricing page before you buy.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Name the cause
plan.text: Read the causes list and pick the one that fits your last stall. Write it at the top of the draft. Then open the file and read only the last paragraph before you write anything new.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Restart mid-sentence
plan.text: Open the draft at your last sentence and finish it. Do not reread earlier chapters. If a fact is missing, put it in brackets so you can move on without solving it now.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Set a session target
plan.text: Set a small session target in Scrivener, or a word goal you track with the word count in Pages, Word, or Google Docs. Write until the target is met, then stop. Keep the goal small enough to finish on a bad day.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Write badly on purpose
plan.text: Write one scene in plain words, with no editing that day. Leave brackets for missing details. If it helps, move the rough scene to a new file so the main draft stays clean.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Keep what moved the draft
plan.text: Check which fix helped most this week. Keep it for next week. Drop the ones that only felt like progress. Write one if-then plan, such as: if it is after lunch, then I write before I check email.
